svg.title: Route targets: the import and export match that decides whether a VPN route enters a VRF
svg.desc: A decision flow on the left: a VPNv4 route arrives carrying one or more route target attributes; the receiving PE compares them with the import list of each VRF; if any RT intersects, the route is imported into that VRF and the local RD is prefixed; if none matches, the route stays in the VPNv4 table and is never installed, which looks identical to no route at all. A right panel shows the two asymmetries that make RTs a policy tool: several RTs may be attached on export so one route reaches many VRFs, and the import list on each side may differ from its export list, which is how hub-and-spoke and one-way extranet are built. A bottom band gives the three-line table to write for every VRF and the warning that RTs are matched exactly, with no wildcard and no automatic translation.
svg.text: A route enters a VRF only if its export RT appears in that VRF's import list
Intersection, not equality: one route can carry several RTs and reach several VRFs
THE IMPORT DECISION
VRF RED import RT 65000:100 → match: imported
VRF BLUE import RT 65000:200 → no match: stays in BGP only
A route with no matching import is invisible in every VRF, and the CE simply has no route.
Why this looks like a bug and is not
The route is in the VPNv4 table, advertised and received. It was never imported. Three tables, three truths.
TWO ASYMMETRIES = THE POLICY TOOL
Many RTs on export
Attach 65000:100 and 65000:900 to one route → it reaches
the customer VRF and the shared-services VRF at once.
Import list different from export list
Hub imports every spoke RT, spokes import only the hub RT.
What this builds, with no extra protocol
Hub-and-spoke: one export, many imports on the hub.
One-way extranet: a partner imports only the shared prefix RT.
Full mesh: every VRF exports and imports one common RT.
THE THREE LINES TO WRITE FOR EVERY VRF — THEN THE DESIGN IS DONE
RD (unique per VRF per PE) · export RT list (what this site offers) · import RT list (what this site may reach).
RTs match exactly: no wildcards, no summarization, no automatic translation between two domains. A typo is a silent black hole.
Design habit that pays for itself: treat the RT plan as an addressing plan. Number it by service, not by customer name, and keep one
authoritative table. Every extranet request then becomes a table edit, reviewed like a firewall rule, instead of a config change on five PEs.
